function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository, followed by a short “cheat‑sheet” of the Git commands you’ll need to run locally to finish the task.

> **NOTE** – I’m unable to clone or push to your GitHub account from here, but the files below are fully functional and you can copy‑paste them into the repo yourself.

---

## 1️⃣  Dockerfile (Node.js)

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Build step (if you have a build script)
# RUN npm run build   # Uncomment if you have a build step

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> - Uses the official `node:18-alpine` image – small, fast, and production‑ready.  
> - Copies `package.json` first so Docker can cache the `npm ci` layer.  
> - Runs `npm ci --only=production` to install only production dependencies.  
> - Exposes port **3000** (the default for many Node apps; adjust if your app uses a different port).  
> - Starts the app with `npm start`.

---

## 2️⃣  Kubernetes YAML (Deployment + Service)

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or any name you prefer) with the following content:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP / NodePort if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> - Deploys **3 replicas** of your app (adjust as needed).  
> - Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster.  
> - Creates a **LoadBalancer** service that forwards external traffic on port 80 to the pods.  
> - Uses an image tag `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`; replace with the actual registry/tag you’ll push to.

---

## 3️⃣  GitHub Actions Workflow (CI/CD)

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        # Uncomment and configure if you want to auto‑deploy after push
        # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
        # with:
        #   manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
        #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
        #   images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **Key points**  
> - Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> - Builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile in the repo root.  
> - Pushes the image to **GitHub Container Registry** (`ghcr.io`).  
> - Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication (no extra secrets required).  
> - Optional deployment step commented out – enable it if you want automatic K8s deployment.

---

## 4️⃣  Git Commands (Run Locally)

Assuming you already cloned the repo locally:

```bash
# 1. Add the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 2. Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions CI"

# 3. Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

If you haven’t cloned yet, do it first:

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
# ... then run the add/commit/push commands above
```

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile added |
| ✅ | Kubernetes YAML added |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow added |
| ✅ | Files staged (`git add`) |
| ✅ | Commit made (`git commit -m "..."`) |
| ✅ | Pushed to `main` (`git push`) |

Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the Docker image, and push it to GHCR. If you enabled the optional deployment step, it will also apply the K8s manifests to your cluster.

Happy coding! 🚀
